record.paper_title: Open Questions in Massive Star Research across Cosmic Scales
record.original_question: What physical mechanism explains why some high-redshift, star-forming galaxies observed with JWST are strongly enriched in nitrogen relative to oxygen and lie between the carbon-nitrogen and carbon-nitrogen-oxygen equilibrium abundance patterns? Candidate explanations to distinguish include unusually efficient and bursty star formation, dense progenitor systems of globular clusters, enrichment sparked by extremely massive or supermassive stars, enrichment by ordinary massive and very massive stars, and systematic problems in abundance diagnostics, stellar-evolution models, or feedback models, especially because high-redshift metallicity measurements are mostly oxygen-based whereas population-synthesis assumptions about stellar evolution depend strongly on iron abundance.

evidence.quote: Yet, the spectra obtained from star-forming galaxies have led to multiple puzzling discoveries that do not fit in our (previous) view about massive stars, most prominently reionization-era galaxies highly enriched in nitrogen (N). Fig. 1 shows a sample of these objects in the N versus oxygen (O) plane. The galaxies are significantly more N-rich than most known star-forming galaxies and H II regions, but all targets essentially are located between the CN and CNO equilibrium which could be reached even if the galaxies are normal in C/O.

Lots of open questions around these findings are currently discussed (e.g., Cameron et al. 2023; Marques-Chaves et al. 2024; Berg et al. 2025; Arellano-Córdova et al. 2025; Morel et al. 2025): Could more efficient and bursty star-formation be responsible? As the high-redshift galaxies are extremely dense, do we maybe see the progenitors of Globular Clusters, possibly sparked by extremely massive stars or even supermassive stars? Or are massive and very massive stars sufficient and the problem in our understanding is rather located in the diagnostics and well as the evolution and feedback models?

In particular the latter is not getting easier by the fact that metallicity measurements at high redshift are essentially all O-based, while population synthesis models include assumptions about stellar evolution that are significantly depending on the iron abundance.

artifact.status_search_result: The origin of the nitrogen-enhanced high-redshift galaxies discovered by JWST (e.g., GN-z11, CEERS-1019, GS_3073) remains an active open question as of 2026. Multiple competing scenarios — supermassive stars, very massive stars, Wolf–Rayet enrichment, globular-cluster progenitors, tidal disruption events, and bursty star formation — are still being debated in the literature, with no single mechanism established as the explanation.

status_evidence.title: Nitrogen enhancements 440 Myr after the Big Bang (Cameron et al.)
status_evidence.snippet: GN-z11 shows extreme N/O; possible enrichment by supermassive stars or runaway collisions in dense clusters; multiple scenarios remain viable.
status_evidence.claim: Multiple unresolved scenarios are proposed for the N-enrichment seen in JWST high-z galaxies.

status_evidence.title: Marques-Chaves et al. 2024, N-emitters at high redshift
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses N-rich galaxies and possible roles of very massive and supermassive stars; conclusions remain inconclusive.
status_evidence.claim: The physical origin of the high N/O is still under discussion in 2024.

status_evidence.title: Morel et al. 2025 / Berg et al. 2025 follow-ups
status_evidence.snippet: Recent works continue to debate diagnostics, stellar evolution, and feedback as sources of systematic uncertainty in interpreting N/O.
status_evidence.claim: As of 2025–2026 the question is still open.
